alfred-green-new-holland-1920-08-09.A1:
SAVED FROM LYNCHERS 2 Welsh Mountain Negroes Locked Up When Farmers Threaten
Lancaster, Pa., Aug. 9. — Charles Smith and Alfred Green, Welsh mountain negroes, were placed in the Lancaster county jail today to prevent the carrying out of lynching threats raised by citizens of New Holland and Intercourse.

The negroes are charged with having robbed a number of homes along the main line and holding up farmers en route to market. The men were armed when captured by state police last night after a spectacular chase through New Holland. Both men have criminal records.

canton-canton-1920-08.A1:
LABOR AGENT KIDNAPED
Canton, Miss, Aug. 18—The city of Canton, known for its peonage farm environments has again been brought into disrepute by the arrest of a prominent colored man, who was employed by the Illinois Central Railroad to secure labor. So anxious are the authorities in this community to prevent our people from leaving the state that they are holding their victim incommunicado after a mock trial and a fine of $500.00. The name of the prisoner has also been withheld from the public. This fine will be worked out on one of the peonage farms of this state which is the usual system of the South, and is largely the cause of the migration of thousands of Negroes to the North. It is said that as a result of this affair, numbers are leaving Canton by night now.

dr-laws-elkins-1920-08-14.A1:
The State Council of the Junior Order is with us this week and holding their 32nd Annual Session, in the Baptist Church. There are about 300 in all from every county in the state. The Delegates began to arrive Monday and Tuesday and the Session opened yesterday morning at 9:30 with all the officers present. The daughters of America, the Womans Branch of the Order are also here and holding their Annual Session at the Odd Fellows Hall. A fine looking lot of women compose this body and they all attended the opening services at the Baptist Church. The usual Committees were announced and both Grand Lodges got down to business with the regular routine work of the order. The Juniors nominated officers for the coming oear and Point Pleasant, Charleston, Clarksburg and Philippi were placed in the nomination for the next place of meeting and these officers and places will be voted on today.

Leland Coberly of this city seems to be in the toils of the Prohibition law. His home was raided and searched by the Prohib Sleuths, this week, Cole Stalnaker, Joe Doerr and a Federal officer and they found some home made wine and some home-brew beer and a little moonshine, all made and for his own use, but it seems to be a violation of the Federal Law and he was held under bond for appearance at the U. S. Court in Martinsburg. The warrant seems to have been issued by U. S Commissioner, Lily of Grafton.

Most people thought that fighting Indians was a thing of the past, but indian warfare broke out again right here in Randolph county last week and peace terms were made here in Elkins. A bunch of what most people thought were gypsies, appeared in Elkins last week, traveling through the country in autos. There were three Ford car loads and one motor truck loaded with tents and camp equipage. This cast doubt on the outfit being Gypsies as they travel with wagons and a lot of old horses to trade on, as horse-trading and fortune telling is their main stock in business, and upon investigation they claimed to be Cherokee Indians on their way from the Ever Glades of Florida to Oklahoma and their cars had Florida State license tags on them. They went on down to Norton and camped on the coal company land and Thursday night a crowd of young fellows attacked them, so they claimed, throwing rocks and cutting the ropes of their tents. They came to Elkins and swore out warrants and the Prosecuting Attorney sent the officers after the crowd and rounded up nine or ten young fellows and brought them before Justice Caplinger of this place. There was much conflicting testimony and the Indians were unable to indentify most of the crowd. They picked out some who admitted to being there and some who were not there. One Italian, who was in it was fined and the other nine boys were dismissed as there was but little reliable evidence against them. The Justice deputised them special officers to guard the camp till Sunday morning when they pulled out westward.

Another race war was started in town Saturday night, this time between the whites and blacks. It seems to have originated with some young fellows from Beverly, who had trouble with some young colored fellows who followed them because they had some "yaller" girls with them. A big fellow came along loaded with moonshine and took it up and had a scrap with one of the colored boys, who got away from him. Later the white fellow who was still hunting trouble had a scrap with Dr. Laws at the John B. Wilt Corner and Laws appealed to the Mayor, who came out to disperse

up which was done by the night policeman and Charley Whetsell. The Mayor gave him a hearing Monday and fined him $15 and costs. Then Dr. Laws was arrested for fighting and was to have a hearing Monday night, and the City Hall was jammed with a crowd to hear it and feeling ran so high that the Mayor postponed the trial till Friday night. Dr. Laws claims that the white man who assaulted him had a knife and some of the crowd claim that Laws had a knife and altogether there is considerable hard feelings and the end is not yet.

S. E. Tiffany, the Supt. of the Gas Company here, takes great delight in flowers and makes a specialty of dahlias and has about seventy different varieties in his yard and garden, surrounding his handsome home in Elkins and it is a treat to visit the place and see this magnificent exhibition of floral beauties. Some of the dahlia stalks are over eight feet high and every color and shade is represented and all sizes and shapes, some of the flowers are as large as sunflowers and measuring ten inches in diameter. Some are shaped like a sunflower and others look like chrysanthemums and various other flowers. This dahlia display would carry off all the prizes at any flower show in the country. Mr. Tiffany cultivates them himself and takes great delight in growing every known variety. One beauty about the dahlia, is they keep on blooming till frost kills them and would bloom the year around in a summer climate.

They are still after Dr. Laws, the colored physician. Tuesday night about 2 o'clock, the police raided his office, under suspicion of a poker game being in progress. There were two City Police and three State Police. The door was locked and when they got in they found four white men and another colored man besides the Doctor. After hunting around they found some cards and "Chips that pass in the night." All the men were released on their own recognizance to appear for trial Saturday night at the Mayors office.

The Junior Order Parade last evening was a big affair. It formed at the Randolph Hotel at 7:30 and headed by the Elkins Band and the military branch of the order and followed by the Daughters of America and Grand Council officers and Delegates and Juniors marched around the principal streets to the Baptist Church, where a splendid public session was held. The church was crowded and a good program was carried out. M. L. Daniels, Chairman of the committee on arrangements presided and called the State Council officers of the Juniors and Daughters of America to the platform. Patriotic airs were sung and Mayor Fredlock delivered an eloquent address of welcome which was responded to by Mr. Seibert of Martinsburg. The Elkins Quartette, Dr. Geo. Neale. Harry Ryan, H. N. Barnard and Will Knapp rendered splendid vocal selections. Boyd Wees was at his best with the "Man Who Went Overseas" and being recalled gave one on "the New Church Choir". Miss Emily Barry gave a splendid reading on the "Cremation of Sam McGee" and received tremendous applause. The Girls Orchestra from the Odd Fellows Home furnished instrumental music and were heartily applauded and a handsome collection taken up for them. All the Grand Lodge officers spoke and the session was a big success.

ensley-ensley-1920-08-19.A2:
DYNAMITERS REPEAT BUT LEAVE NO CLUE
Another Negro House Wrecked. Two Men Hurt
The last one occurred about 2 o'clock yesterday afternoon, when a house occupied by negroes at Alley H and Twenty-first street, Ensley, was almost completely wrecked by a dynamite detonation.
Two negro men who lived in the house were seriously injured by the explosion. They were taken to the emergency hospital at Ensley.
Officers who are investigating the incidents say that as yet they have found no trace of a clue that will lead to a motive. The explosion completely wrecked two rooms of the house and only left standing one or two walls on the other side of the house.
ensley-ensley-1920-08-19.A3:
NEGRO DYNAMITES
HOUSE FOR REVENGE
Dwelling House With Four
Occupants Blown Up By
Jealous Husband
Coleman McShants, negro, has been arrested and placed in the Ensley jail for blowing up a negro house in the alley between Avenue H and Avenue I Thursday morning at 2 o'clock. McShants is said to have confessed following his arrest by Officers Millicen and Tyler.

The house, which was a two-room building, was completely demolished, the floor and all of the furniture in the room under which the dynamite was placed being entirely destroyed. The room was occupied by Melissa Mitchell and her twelve-year-old son, who escaped death by a miracle. They were carried to the Ensley infirmary, where they were found to be greatly shocked, but only slightly injured. Two women who occupied the rear room were uninjured.

McShants and his wife had been separated and dynamiting the house was his method of getting revenge.
This is the second attempt to blow up a building in the Ensley district during the past ten days. The store and house of Tony Antonio on Avenue F was partly demolished by dynamite being placed under the front porch.
ensley-ensley-1920-08-19.A4:
NOTED MISSISSIPPIAN VISITS HARDING
MARION, O., August 20.—Isaiah T. Montgomery of Mound Bayou, Miss., and the founder of that exclusively Colored town, was here last Friday for a conference with Senator Harding. After the conference, Mr. Montgomery left for Chicago, where he will confer with Henry Lincoln Johnson, of Georgia, who is head of the Colored bureau of the national committee.

ENSLEY, Ala., Sept. 1.—For the second time in two weeks, the home of a Colored family living at Alley H and Twenty-first street, was dynamited last Thursday morning. The police have been unable to capture the dynamiters.

DOTHAN NOTES
DOTHAN, ALA., Aug. 11.—A reunion of the well known Riley family of Midland City was held here Tuesday. There were eight sisters and two brothers, together with their children and grandchildren present. The following are the children: Mrs. A. A. Odom, Greenville, S. C., Miss Hattie Riley, Greenville, S. C., Mrs. S. M. C. Howell, Midland City, Ala., Mrs. Malcolm Grace, Ozark, Ala., Mrs. J. L. Hunt, Echo, Ala., Mrs. J. R. Levy, Ozark Ala., Mrs. W. S. Coleman, Midland City, Ala., Messrs J. E. Z. Riley, Ozark, and J. J. Riley, Cottonwood, Ala. The reunion was held at the home of Mr. and Mrs. W. S. Palmer in Midland City.

Edith Herlong Dies.

Edith Herlong, age 6, died early Tuesday morning at her home in Clayton from pneumonia which followed an operation for removal of tonsils. The little girl was a niece of Mrs. W. H. King, of this city, who left immediately to attend the funeral.

Negro Is Lynched.

Monroe Wood, a negro, was lynched near Newville in Henry county, for insulting a white woman one day last week, according to a report reaching Dothan Tuesday. The negro is said to have been caught north of Newville and shot to death by a mob.

Memorial Service.

There will be a memorial service for confederate dead at Liberty Church, Pansy, Ala., Saturday, Aug. 21. A special program has been arranged for the occasion which includes speeches and a sermon at 10 a. m. The memorial services and parade start at 11 o'clock and will be followed by dinner on the ground.

J. V. LeGruy, treasurer of the federal land bank at New Orleans, is in Dothan the guest of A. Y. Malone, former treasurer of the same institution. This is Mr. LeGruy's first visit here and he expressed himself as delighted with this section.

percy-thompson-meridian-1920-08.A1:
MERIDIAN, MISS.
Meridian, Miss., August 1.—(Special.) The criminal terms of the Lauderdale county circuit court to be convened in Meridian tomorrow by Judge C. C. Miller, in all probability will be one of the most interesting in many years because of the number and character of some of the crimes.

It will be the first term to be held by Judge Miller, who was appointed by Governor Russell to preside until a special election can be held to elect a successor for the full term of Judge Rowland Heidelberg, resigned. Judge Miller is one of Meridian's foremost lawyers, son of the late C. C. Miller, who was a leading lawyer of the state As he is a candidate for the full term his conduct of the court will be filled with interest and watched eagerly by his friends and supporters.

It will become his duty to deliver a charge to the grand jury for investigation of crime in this county and included in those to be probed are three of the foulest murders ever committed in this section of the state, one lynching and two attempted lynchings that have occurred since the last session of the criminal court in February.

The murders to receive the attention of the grand jury are those of James A. Tyral, suburban merchant, who was shot and fatally wounded in his store. On the same night the murder of Henry W. Davis, aged night watchman at a local lumber plant, was shot to death and robbed. For the commission of these crimes two negroes, Henry Llovd and Will Echols, were arrested and taken to Jackson, where they have been held in jail for fear that they might be lynched. One of the negroes, since arrest, the officers say, has confessed, implicating the other. The next murder to horrify the county was that of Miss Carrie Hatcher, eighteen-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George W. Hatcher, who was mysteriously choked to death near her home and her body thrown into a small brook.

The grand jury is also to probe the lynching of James Spencer, negro postal clerk, following his attack on Otto Parker, white postal clerk, while the two were on duty in the same car; the attempted lynching of Percy Thompson, for attempted criminal assault on a young Syrian girl, and the attempted lynching of Ludie Martin, arrested as a suspect in the Hatcher murder case. There are also a number of other criminal cases to receive attention, such as burglary and robbery.
percy-thompson-meridian-1920-08.A2:
GRAND JURY TOLD
TO GO AFTER MOB
New Circuit Judge Delivers Ringing Charge When Jury Is Sworn In
Meridian. Miss., August 2.—(Special.)—Circuit Judge C. C. Miller, assuming the bench for the first time today following his appointment by Governor Russell to succeed to the vacancy caused by the resignation of Judge Rowland W. Heidelberg, delivered a ringing charge to the grand jury when that body was sworn in after opening the criminal term of the Lauderdale county circuit court. He charged the jury specially with reference to the recent lynching of James Spencer, negro postal clerk, by a small party of masked men when the prisoner was being taken to Enterprise, in Clarke county, to answer to a charge of assault with intent on Otho Parker, white postal clerk, while the two were at work in their car as it passed through that county. He also called the jury's special attention to recent attempts by mobs of unmasked white men to force the county jail here in an effort to get possession of Percy Thompson, negro, charged with attempted criminal assault on a young Syrian girl, and Ludie Martin, arrested as a suspect in connection with the murder of Miss Carrie Hatcher, 18-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George W. Hatcher, prosperous planter residing a few miles from Meridian, the girl having been choked to death and her body cast by the murderers into a brook in a pasture near the Hatcher home. Judge Miller, in referring to the reckless disregard of the law by mobs, asked the jury to exert every effort to bring the guilty parties to justice, and he would see that the law is vindicated. With W. T. Rainey, planter, as foreman, the remaining members of the grand jury are as follows: H. E. Curtis, L. E. Cobb, R. S. Kinard, Amos Brunson, J. L. Welch, I. P. Vincent, D. L. Little, J. W. Stanton, W. L. Denton, J. E. Bond, H. F. Gabriel, N. D. Camp, J. A. Butler, J. W. Barham, A. F. Ellis,

MERIDIAN, MISS.
Meridian, Miss., August 13.—(Special.)—The criminal term of the Lauderdale county circuit court was adjourned today by Judge C. C. Miller after being in session only ten days. The term has been one of the most important in years, about seventy-eight cases being disposed of. Among these were the cases of Henry Lloyd and Will Echols, negroes, charged with the murder of white men, and sentenced to be hanged, the former September 3 and the latter September 10. Percy Thompson, negro, sentenced to imprisonment for attempted criminal assault on a young Syrian girl of Meridian, and a number of lesser convictions and sentences.

Congressman Collier and Mayor Hayes of Vicksburg were the guests here last night of the local Odd Fellows when an entertaining programme by local talent was rendered. There were a number of short talks made but the principal addresses were made by the Vicksburg visitors.

Friends of former Attorney General Rose Collins are arranging for a big political demonstration in his behalf Saturday night when he delivers the first speech of his campaign for Congress in this city. It is announced that there will be many citizens here from practically every one of the ten counties of the district to participate in the demonstration. The friends of Congressman Venable are also preparing a demonstration in his behalf for Monday night, his address on that occasion closing the campaign before the first primary, which will be held on Tuesday. Both speeches will be delivered from platforms erected on the street in the business district. C. C. Johnson, the third candidate in the race for Congress, delivered an address tonight from a platform in the street to a fair-sized audience. Te vote he will get has all the wise ones guessing because it may cause a second primary between Collins and Venable.

robert-williams-lynchburg-1920-08-15.A1:
ARRESTS NEGRO CHARGED
WITH ATTACKING WOMAN
Lynchburg Governess Will Make Effort to Identify Assailant When She Recovers.
(Special to The Times Dispatch.)
LYNCHBURG, VA. August 7.—A

(LYNCHBURG, VA., August 7.—As soon as Miss Annie Ross, who was criminally attacked by a negro last night at 11:30, sufficiently recovers from her experience she will be asked to look at Robert Williams, alias "Alabama Red," in an effort to identify him as her assailant. She still is under care of a physician, but is expected to look the negro over in a day or two.

Miss Ross, who came here a few years ago from Sweden, is a professional massuese and is of athletic build, but, despite the fight she made she was unable to free herself until she had been dragged about 200 yards to a secluded spot and overpowered by the negro.

In her struggle with the negro her clothes were torn and there were bruises and scratches on her body. As soon as she reached the Haley home the alarm was given and a posse, assisted by the police, began a prompt search for the assailant. Chief of Police John Seay, taking personal charge of the hunt.

Miss Ross said the negro struck her with a wrench, and in the home of Williams was found a wrench with mud on it. Officers also claim they found other evidence corroborative of their belief that Williams is the right man. He now is in jail awaiting identification.

Williams was arrested this morning after bloodhounds had followed a trail from the scene of the attack in Rivermont, near Randolph-Macon Woman's College, to a house in Chambersville, a negro suburb, where Williams lived alone.

Williams was at home at the time and was immediately placed under arrest, although denying guilt.

Miss Ross, a governess in the home of E. F. Haley, was seized on North Princeton Street, shortly after she had left a Rivermont car from downtown, where she attended a moving-picture show.

Nor, was it known that the negro had been taken out of the city until during the day today.

robert-williams-lynchburg-1920-08-15.A6:
JAILER HIDES
MAN FROM MOB
Then Unmasks "Leader"
And Places Him in Cell Of Prisoner.
Lynchburg, Va., Aug. 15.—After an early morning attack on the jail by a mob of over 300, Robert Williams, colored, charged with criminal assault on Miss Annie Ross, was spirited to Roanoke today.

The mob was met at the jail gate by Jailer Tyree and a few policemen.

"We want Williams," yelled the leader, who had a handkerchief around his face to conceal his identity.

"You'll play h—— getting him," retorted one of the officers who, with a quick jerk, pulled the handkerchief away, revealing a prominent citizen of Lynchburg.

The officer then shoved the man through the jail gate and he was lodged in the same cell from which the negro had been removed a few minutes before.

Another member of the mob was arrested a few minutes later. It then broke up.
robert-williams-lynchburg-1920-08-15.A7:
FOIL JAIL MOB,
ARREST CHIEFS
Negro Is Spirited Away From Would-Be Lynchers—Admits Attack on Woman.
LYNCHBURG, Va., Aug. 16.—Robert: Williams, negro, charged with assault upon Miss Annie Ross here ten days ago, confessed yesterday, first to the police and later to Mayor Jester, following which he was taken to the Roanoke jail.

All of this followed the effort of a leaderless mob of 200 or 300 persons to take him from the jail for a lynching, Saturday night. Williams was not in the jail at the time, having been spirited away by Chief of Police Seay, who kept him in hiding until time for the last night train to Roanoke. No trouble was experienced in getting Williams out of the city.

The mob formed and went to the jail about 1 o'clock. It was met by Jailer Tyree and a few policemen. Tyree, jerked a handkerchief from the face of one of the leaders and landed him in the cell from which Williams had but recently been hurried. Another member of the mob was pushed into the jail and then the lynchers broke. In a few minutes practically everybody had left the vicinity.

The two men arrested are O. H. Morris and Aubrey Foster. The mob appears to have been composed mostly of young men and it lacked leadership.

Almost immediately the mob swooped down on the jail. The organization was perfect up to that time, for the leaders of the mob were cowed by Tyree, an old-time police officer, and Chief of Police Seay.

A hurry call quickly brought officers from all parts of the city, and after Morris and Foster were locked up the men who made up the crowd quickly dispersed, not knowing at the time that the negro was not inside the jail.

It is believed Judge Christian will return and issue a call immediately for a special term of his court, as ordinarily there would be no court until September 7. That he will also order a rigid investigation to ascertain the identity of more members of the mob, is thought certain.
robert-williams-lynchburg-1920-08-15.A10:
Mob Members Fined.
Mob Members Fined.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
LYNCHBURG, VA., August 18.—Charged with committing "unlawful assembly, and riot," O. H. Morris and Aubrey Foster, two young men, who were arrested early Sunday morning out of the crowd which gathered before the city jail for the purpose of securing Robert Williams, the negro who has confessed to attacking a white woman, for a lynching, were convicted in the Police Court today and were fined $25 each and sentenced to ten days in jail.

robert-williams-lynchburg-1920-08-15.A12:
REWARD PROPOSED
FOR HOUND OWNER
Lynchburg, Va., Aug. 21.—When the two branches of the city council meet in called sessions next week they will have before them a recommendation from Mayor Jester that the city pay F. T. Fortune, owner of a blood-hound kennel here, $500 for his success in running down Robert Williams, the negro who has since confessed to criminal assault.

The people generally now believe that Williams is not in the jail here, but it is universally admitted that it would be unwise to return him here for trial without military protection.
robert-williams-lynchburg-1920-08-15.A15:
Williams was found guilty by the jury after deliberating only eight minutes.
He was brought to Lynchburg from Roanoke, where he has been confined since an effort to lynch him last month. It was not generally known that he would be tried yesterday, and this fact was not advertised for fear of an attempt to take him away from the officers.
When his case was called considerable surprise was manifest among the few spectators.
The negro pleaded not guilty. He repudiated previous signed confessions in the hands of the police.
There was no cross-examination and the defense did not argue the case.
Williams will be electrocuted at the State penitentiary at Richmond, November 13.

sills-spinks-grimes-1920-07-29.A1:
FURTHER RACE CLASH IN DALE MAY RESULT Third Negro Is Shot; Lodge Hall Burned; Spinks' Wife Leaves County
(Special to the Advertiser.)

OZARK, ALA., July 31.—Further trouble between the whites and negroes in the Grimes neighborhood, near the Dale-Houston line, is momentarily expected despite the efforts being made to control the situation and calm the passions of those who have sought to mete out justice following the murderous attack upon Mrs. L. E. Dassenger Thursday night and which was followed by the lynching of two negroes, SiHs Spinks and Juster Jennings.

Casualties added to the above as a result of this attack included the beating of two negro women in a sporadic outbreak Friday and was followed, it was learned here today, by the shooting of a third negro man, Richard Jones, Friday night, his arm and leg having been broken, while another was given a severe whipping. A negro judge hall near Grimes was made the object of a torch and destroyed during the night also.

The wife of Andrew Spinks, a negro held at Montgomery on a charge of attempted criminal assault, over which it is said the vicious attack on Mrs. Dassenger resulted, was given twenty-four hours to leave the county today and another negro also received similar orders, it was reported.

All negroes have been warned to stay in their homes and law-abiding members of the race are being given full protection. Sheriff Gamble has been constantly on the scene of the Grimes lynching to stop any untoward activities, and tonight held the opinion that further trouble might be averted.

Coroner White who conducted an investigation into the death of Spinks and Jennings, whose bodies were left lying in a public road until Friday morning, had not divulged any information as to opinions connecting white residents of the county with the double-affair. The bitter feeling that was aroused over Andrew Spinks' action some weeks ago, maintains here and trouble may break out if he is brought here for trial in August as per present plans.

Montgomery, Ala., July 30.—Two negro men, Sills Spinks and J. Jennings are dead, two women severely wounded from beatings and a thoroughly alarmed negro population at Grimes, a small rural community on the Dale-Houston county line summarizes the activities of posses who went out Thursday night after Spinks, who late in the evening assaulted Mrs. L. Mrs. Dassenger, alone in her home at the time of the attack, was approached from behind and felled by a heavy weapon in the hands of Sills Spinks, who, it is alleged, declared to the woman that she would never live to testify against his father, Andrew Spinks, who is held in the Montgomery county jail charged with attempting to criminally assault her. MOB BRUTALLY BEATS AGED WOMAN
Montgomery, Ala., Aug. 4.—Despite the conscious efforts of the leading white and colored citizens of the South to eradicate the mob spirit it continues to reign supreme in many parts of lynchland. A posse of blood-thirsty cannibals while searching for Sills Spinks and J. Jennings, colored, supposed assailants of Mrs. L. E Dossenger (white), brutally heats three of the most highly respected colored women in Gimes, a small rural community on the outskirts of Montgomery.

After they had beaten the innocent women, they were not satisfied, but continued to go from house to house until they had caused a general alarm. The next morning they met Jennings and Spinks on their way to work and riddled their bodies with bullets. A the inquest it was found that there was no evidence whatsoever to connect either of the men with the supposed crime.

The feeling is very high according to the latest reports. The coloree people are very resentful. The lower element is armed to the teeth waiting a chance to avenge the death of the innocent men. The other elements are leaving for the North and East by the hundreds.

Dothan, Ala., July 30.—Sills Spinks and Jester Jennings, Negroes, were shot to death by members of a posse at Midland City, near here last night, after an attempt to kill the wife of a white farmer. The Negroes of the little town had been rounded up in an effort to identify the woman's assailant, according to reports reaching here, when the shooting occurred.

Andy Spinks, father of Sills Spinks is in jail, at Montgomery, charged with attacking the same woman several months ago. She is to be the principal witness in the case.

300 PEOPLE TESTIFY BEFORE GRAND JURY Report on Dale County Lynching May Be Rendered Dur- ing Day (Special to the Advertiser.)
OZARK, Aug. 18.—Fully three hundred people from the Midland City and Grimes community were before the grand jury now in session, Tuesday and Wednesday to tell what they knew of the lynching of the two negroes, Sills Spinks and Buster Jennings in this county on July 30th.

The large crowd was orderly and throughout the two days no disturbance of any kind was had. The woman who was assaulted, appeared before the body Tuesday afternoon.

The jury at this time have not given out any information but it is thought that it will make a partial report Thursday morning. People were seen in small crowds about the court house during the two days' session, but nothing could be learned from them.

The warrants for the arrest of the three white men, who are said to be the ones responsible for one of the negroes death, have not been executed, the officers waiting upon the action of the grand jury.

The matter is being investigated thoroughly and the body will go to the "bottom" of the lynching carrying out the instructions of the presiding judge

ANDREW SPINKS GETS 20 YEAR PENAL TERM FOR CRIMINAL ATTACK Assailant of Dale County Woman Pleads Guilty At Ozark
OZARK, ALA., Aug. 26—Andrew Spinks, negro, brought here this morning from the Montgomery county jail, for arraignment on a charge of criminal assault upon a white woman of Dale county, entered a plea of guilty to the charge in circuit court this afternoon and was sentenced to 20 years in the State penitentiary by Judge J. S. Williams.

An enormous crowd had gathered at Ozark for the trial of Spinks, who narrowly escaped lynching after the commission of the crime with which he was charged and had been indicted for. By sheer nerve and ingenuity Sheriff Gamble had spirited his prisoner out of the county before it was well known that he had been taken, carrying him first to the Pike county jail and then to Montgomery for safe-keeping.

Over 1,000 people from the Grimes and Midland City sections of the county, where the crime occurred, alone, were present today and had the jail surrounded when the sheriff reached town with his prisoner. No effort to molest the negro or interfere with the due course of the law, was manifest however, and it was apparent that the people would be satisfied with a heavy penalty.

Spinks' conviction bringing to a close a sensational chapter of Dale county's life, which commenced with the attack on the white woman, who resides near Grimes, was followed by a murderous assault upon her by the son of Andrew Spinks, which in turn resulted in the lynching of the son, Sills Spinks and Buster Jennings, the burning of the negro lodge hall near Midland City, the administering of severe whippings to several other nogroes and forcible ejection of others from the county.

LYNCHING BRINGS ALARM TO SOUTH
(By Staff Correspondent.)
OZARK, ALA. Aug. 25—Evidence that the economic pressure being brought to bear on account of the wave of lynching now prevailing in the South is bearing fruit was apparent at the Dale County Circuit Court when Judge J. S. Williams, presiding over the fall session, instructed the grand jury to go to the very roots of the lynching of two colored men, Sill Spinks and Juster Jenkins, on the night of July 30, near Grimes, Ala.

Huge Crowds Attend Court.

Huge crowds were present watching every move made, and it is said that witnesses, have been summoned from Midland, Grimes, and that territory. It is claimed that the sentiment is divided between those who wish to see the South rid of the lynch epidemic and those who fear indictment for the lynching.

Report Evidence to Indict Several.

It is said that evidence has been reported which will, probably, result in the indictment of several sons of the leading men of this community, and much speculation is being made as to whether these men will receive immunity on account of their connections.

Migration Has Impoverished County.

It is thought that the present investigations are due not so much to the change in spirit of the Southerners as to the fact that this county has been practically impoverished by the migration of our race. Fully 10,000 colored people deserted the county immediately after the lynchings, and agriculture is at a standstill. Circular letters have been sent many of the colored people of the vicinity asking them to remain as a patriotic duty. An ironical feature is that most of the recipients can neither read nor write, on account of the fact that the South's educational program does not include the Negro. The circulars thus miss their mark.

Flimsy Identity
Further trouble between the races is momentarily expected because the white men of the city have been attacking every woman of the race who appears on the street. They are beating them, it is claimed, unmercifully. The trouble began when the rumor gained wide circulation that Mrs. L. E. Dassenger (white) was murderously attacked. When interviewed, Mrs. Dassenger declared she "thought the man who assaulted her was colored." She saw his foot and "judged by the size of it that her assailant was a laborer." Spinks and Jennings were found on the street conversing a block away from the house and were seized by the mob. They were not permitted to make any statement and died without knowing what crime they were charged with.
